messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 63
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Oceania
  relationship_status: Divorced
  occupation: Community Organizer
  trauma_type: Life-threatening accident
  pcl5: 49

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Expressions of Anger: Other people expressing anger, even calmly, Intrusive Thoughts: Unwanted thoughts, Visual (Uniforms): Military or police uniforms
  Memory: Partial Clarity: Some moments of the event are extremely clear while others are completely blank, Memory Gaps: There are parts of the event that I simply cannot remember no matter how hard I try, Cannot Find Words: I know what happened but I am unable to find words to describe it
  Negative Appraisals: Emotional Numbness: I feel dead inside, Self-Blame: The event happened because of the way I acted, Body as Enemy: My body keeps reacting as if I am still in danger even when I am safe

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Leilani’s father, a Samoan chief and longshoreman, used to say that a man’s anger was like a reef—visible only when the tide went out. For sixty-three years, Keoni had believed that. He had built a life around it, first as a union steward and then as a community organizer in the Pacific Islander enclave of Carson, California, where his job was to channel other people’s frustrations into petitions and press releases. He was good at it. He knew how to sit with a room full of angry tenants and let the heat dissipate until someone said, “Okay, what do we do next?” That skill had made him respected. It had also, he was now certain, nearly killed him.

The accident happened eighteen months ago, on a Tuesday evening in November. Keoni had been driving home from a housing rights meeting at a church in Compton. At a four-way stop, a black sedan with a cracked windshield ran the intersection at nearly fifty miles per hour. Keoni’s truck flipped twice before landing on its roof in a drainage ditch. He remembers the sound of the sedan’s engine—a high, straining whine like a trapped animal—and the smell of gasoline and the wet earth of the ditch. He remembers the weight of his own body pressing against the seatbelt, the way the blood from a cut on his scalp ran into his left eye and made the world look like it was bleeding. He does not remember the impact itself. He does not remember the paramedics cutting him out of the truck. He does not remember his daughter’s face when she arrived at the hospital, though she tells him she held his hand for three hours. Those hours are simply gone, like pages torn from a book. What remains is a series of snapshots, each one vivid and isolated: the black sedan’s grille filling his windshield, the sensation of the truck’s roof buckling inward above his head, the cold mud against his cheek after he crawled out. Between these images there is only a blank, grey static.

In the months that followed, Keoni discovered that his body had become a stranger. He would be standing at the stove making oatmeal and his heart would begin to pound, his palms slick with sweat, his throat tight as if someone were pressing on his trachea. There was no trigger he could name, no thought that preceded it. His body was reacting as if he were still in that ditch, still pinned by the steering column, and no amount of reasoning could make it stop. He began to feel that his own flesh had betrayed him. He would sit in his small apartment in the evenings, staring at the wall, and realize he had not felt anything for hours—not sadness, not anger, not even the dull satisfaction of a day’s work. Inside, there was only a kind of hollow stillness, as if the emotional part of him had been scooped out like the flesh of a papaya. He told his doctor he felt dead, and the doctor prescribed a sleeping pill and told him to give it time.

Time did not help. Keoni’s work as a community organizer became impossible. At a neighborhood council meeting, a young mother stood up and began to describe, with controlled fury, how her landlord had turned off the hot water. Her voice was steady, her face calm, but her anger was unmistakable. Keoni felt his chest seize. The room seemed to tilt. He excused himself and walked out, leaving the meeting mid-agenda. He could not explain it to his colleagues. He could not explain to himself why a woman’s righteous anger felt like the black sedan bearing down on him. He began to avoid meetings entirely, claiming he had appointments or that he was working on grant applications from home. He stopped answering calls from the tenants’ union. He stopped checking his email. The organization that had once been the center of his life began to function without him, and he let it.

The uniforms were worse. One afternoon at the grocery store, he rounded an aisle and found himself face-to-face with a Los Angeles County Sheriff’s deputy buying a bag of chips. The deputy was young, maybe twenty-five, and he smiled at Keoni in a friendly way. Keoni’s vision narrowed. The fluorescent lights seemed to buzz louder. He left his cart in the middle of the aisle and walked out of the store, his hands shaking. He knew, intellectually, that the deputy had nothing to do with his accident. But his body did not know that. His body knew only that the uniform meant danger, meant the flashing lights he could not remember but could feel, meant the cold metal of the gurney pressing into his back. He began to plan his errands around avoiding certain streets, certain parking lots, certain hours of the day when police presence was higher.

He blamed himself. This was the thought that circled back most often, late at night when the sleeping pill had worn off. He should have seen the sedan. He should have looked both ways twice. He had been in a hurry to get home, and his hurry had caused this. The accident happened because of the way he acted—because he was impatient, because he was careless, because he had not been paying enough attention. He knew this was irrational; the other driver had been drunk and had fled the scene. But the feeling of responsibility was stronger than any fact. It sat in his chest like a stone.

What finally brought Keoni to the clinic was his daughter. She had driven down from San Jose to check on him, and she had found him sitting in the dark at three in the afternoon, the television off, staring at nothing. She had knelt in front of him and said, “Dad, you’re not okay,” and he had started to cry—not from sadness, but from the sudden, shocking sensation of feeling anything at all. He agreed to see a therapist because he did not know what else to do, and because he was afraid that if he did not, the hollow feeling would swallow him completely. He is not sure what he hopes for. He does not think he can get the moments back that he has lost, or make his body stop its strange alarms. But he is tired of being afraid of a woman’s anger, tired of avoiding the grocery store, tired of the way his own heart feels like an enemy. He wants to know if it is possible to feel alive again, or if that part of him is gone for good.
